newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU to push on against U.S. over Cuba sanctions.
newsitem.headline: EU to push on against U.S. over Cuba sanctions.

text.p: The European Union signalled its determination on Saturday to push a potentially explosive World Trade Organisation challenge over the controversial U.S. Helms-Burton law on Cuba unless Washington shifts its position.

EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference that the policy had been unanimously endorsed by a meeting of the 15-nation bloc's trade ministers in Geneva late on Friday and he indicated that the EU retained full support from most other members of the WTO.

Brittan said the latest bid to solve the problem in contacts with U.S. officials had produced no proposals that would meet EU concerns and, in the absence of a change, members of a WTO dispute panel would be named next Thursday.
"That is what will happen on the 20th of February unless we resolve our differences," he said.

On Friday he told reporters that the two powers were "really quite a long way from" a deal that would to head off the move -- an action that would start the clock ticking for a ruling by the three-man panel within six months.
Brittan said that what Brussels was asking of the United States was "moderate and reasonable.... would be lawful under American law, (and) would not necessitate a change in acts of Congress".

The Helms-Burton law, signed by President Bill Clinton a year ago after Cuba shot down two small planes flown by anti-communist exiles near the island, aims to restrict foreign investment in the economy of the communist-ruled country.

The EU, Canada, Mexico and many other trading powers have denounced the legislation as an attempt to impose U.S. law on foreign companies dealing with Havana by leaving them open to prosecution in U.S. courts.

But Brittan made clear on Saturday the EU was also pressing Washington over a similar U.S. Congressional bill named for its sponsor, Senator Alfonse D'Amato of New York, which imposes sanctions on foreign companies investing in Iraq and Iran's oil industries.

Critics of both U.S. measures say they violate Washington's open trade commitments under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the treaty which lies at the foundation of the two-year-old WTO.

In WTO discussion of the Helms-Burton law, which Washington says is aimed at bringing freedom to Cuba by hastening the departure of President Fidel Castro, U.S. officials have argued it is covered by a "national security" clause in the GATT.

Brittan said on Saturday the EU did not accept this argument as valid. Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy told a U.S. audience on Friday that the U.S. stance could subvert the WTO and slow global economic progress.

Many trade diplomats and officials have expressed concern that, if the case is pushed to a conclusion in the WTO and if the panel finds against Washington, it could have serious repercussions on the organisation.

Officials of the Clinton administration have openly warned that the EU action already is strengthening the arguments of Congressional opponents of open trade and global cooperation through the WTO who say the body threatens U.S. sovereignty.

But EU and Canadian officials counter that, if the United States is not challenged, any other member of the WTO could break the body's rules on the claim of "national security", bringing chaos to the world trading system.

The United States has indicated that it will decline to cooperate with a panel, and had earlier refused to approve names put up by the WTO Secretariat, leading the EU to exercise its right to ask Ruggiero to appoint the members himself.
Last week Brussels had asked him to postpone action for another week, until February 20, to give time for more talks.
